meta: A seated couple and three children in a family group attributed to Joshua Johnson, about 1800, now at the National Gallery of Art.
about: A man in a dark coat and yellow waistcoat sits beside a woman in a gray dress who holds a folded paper, and three children stand close by. The painting is attributed to Joshua Johnson and dated about 1800. It was in the hands of Helena Penrose of Southbury, Connecticut, until a sale there in 1964. Agents John Bihler and Henry Coger then bought it for Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch. The Garbisches left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1980.
credit_line: Gift of Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch

meta: Ann Perry Rodgers in a miniature by Anson Dickinson, wife of Commodore George Washington Rodgers and sister of Oliver Hazard Perry.
about: Dark ringlets and a sheer white dress mark Ann Perry Rodgers in this oval miniature by Anson Dickinson. She also wears a coral bead necklace, and a red drape lies over her shoulders. The museum says her marriage in 1815 to Commodore George Washington Rodgers joined two prominent naval families of Annapolis. Her brother was Oliver Hazard Perry. Her husband's family owned the building that is now the Rodgers Tavern in Perryville, Maryland. A grant from the Smithsonian Women's Committee paid for conservation of the miniature.

meta: The Great Rosary by Erhard Schön, a crowded print with the crucifixion at its centre and rows of saints and prophets around it.
about: At the centre of this crowded print is the crucifixion, ringed by flowers. Rows of figures on either side map out the ranks of heaven and earth. God appears above the cross, with the Madonna to the left and angels to the right. Angels hold up the Veronica cloth at the top. Moses and various saints can be picked out among the figures of the rosary. Below, angels pull people from flames. The date 1519 and the monogram MTR sit on a scroll at the upper right.

meta: A handscroll of the four seasons signed by Tosa Mitsuoki, a Kyoto court painter who mixed Tosa and Kano brushwork.
about: A thatched house stands by a stream under drooping willows and bamboo on this silk handscroll, and figures gather beneath cherry blossom on green mounds. The scroll carries a signature and seal. The museum places Tosa Mitsuoki in the Tosa school, painters who had enjoyed the patronage of the imperial court. After he moved to Kyoto in 1634, the school drew new attention. In 1654 he became head of the official Bureau of Painting. He added brushwork from the Kano school to the classical Tosa subjects.

meta: A young woman with a cage of fireflies, a hanging scroll in the manner of Harunobu painted by Shiba Kokan.
about: A young woman in a patterned green kimono stands on a veranda and looks at a caged firefly on a summer night. Shiba Kokan is better known for Western learning and European painting methods, so a beauty in the ukiyo-e style is rare from him. The museum says he imitates Suzuki Harunobu. Kokan wrote in his diary that he forged Harunobu paintings after the master died. This scroll bears the Harunobu seal and is signed Shotei Harushige, a name Harunobu gave him.

meta: A still life with a fan, roses and a stoneware jug by Thomas Hovenden, who mostly painted genre scenes.
about: Roses stand in a stemmed glass beside a tall brown jug, a round painted fan and a porcelain cup with gilt scrollwork. Thomas Hovenden painted a few still lifes in addition to his better-known genre scenes. The museum says the casual arrangement hides careful balance. The arc of blooms at the lower right echoes the details of the Japanese fan. Clear light and luminous shadows, it adds, recall Dutch still life, a tradition Hovenden probably knew from his Paris teachers and from museums.

meta: Francesco del Cossa's Saint Florian, made for Floriano Griffoni's chapel in San Petronio in Bologna and given to the National Gallery of Art in 1939.
about: Floriano Griffoni commissioned this panel of Saint Florian for a family chapel in the church of San Petronio in Bologna. Giorgio Vasari mentions the altarpiece first. About 1731 it moved to the Casa Aldrovandi, and by 1782 it was gone from there. Count Ugo Beni of Gubbio owned it by 1858. It was sold in 1882 as a Saint Martin by Zoppo and in Berlin in 1929 as a different saint. The Samuel H. Kress Foundation bought it from Duveen Brothers in 1936.

meta: Fishermen and families on the shore at Chiaia near Naples, a watercolour by Saverio della Gatta signed in 1828.
about: Three men move a boat lying on the shore at the left. At the right a woman stands spinning, another sits nursing a baby with a girl beside her, and a child eats. A rock rises at the left, and a promontory with a building stands at the right. Capri and the Sorrento peninsula lie in the background. The signature in the lower right corner reads Gatta f. 1828.

meta: Anne Flaxman, née Denman, in a 1797 portrait by Henry Howard at the National Portrait Gallery.
about: A woman turns three-quarters to the right in a pale draped turban over curled hair. She wears a dark ribbon at the throat and a white lace-trimmed collar with a sheer scarf. Henry Howard painted her in 1797. She was born Anne Denman and married in 1782 at the age of 27. The gallery's note calls her well educated and says she assisted her husband throughout his career and was his devoted companion on his travels.

meta: A round tortoiseshell box with a watercolour miniature on its lid, in the Musée Cognacq-Jay, attributed to François Dumont.
about: The box is round and made of blond tortoiseshell, with mouldings in gold of three colours: pink, green and dark grey. On the lid is a miniature in watercolour and gouache on ivory, ringed in gold. It shows a young woman with powdered blue-grey hair and a blue dress with white lace ruffles, seated beside a framed mirror. The Musée Cognacq-Jay in Paris keeps the box.

meta: Abundance, a sketch by José del Castillo for a cartoon in the rooms of Charles III in the Royal Palace, Madrid.
about: A seated woman crowned with flowers holds a sheaf of wheat and a cornucopia spilling grapes and fruit. Putti pick grapes from a tree and rest on the cloud beside her. José del Castillo painted this as one of four preparatory sketches for cartoons. They belonged to the decoration of six overdoors in the conversation room of King Charles III in the Royal Palace in Madrid. The designs follow allegories that Corrado Giaquinto painted for a similar room at the Aranjuez palace. The figures carry symbols that allude to the Apocalypse.

meta: Summer and Winter Landscapes, a pair of six-panel screens by Kano Naonobu at the Cleveland Museum of Art.
about: Summer fills the right screen and winter the left. The composition is sparse, in ink on gold and silver. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the pair was once damaged, and that conservators later added new sections of paper and inpainted them to keep the original feel of the paintings. Kano Naonobu was born in Kyoto, the younger brother of Kano Tanyu. At the request of the Tokugawa government he moved to Edo in 1630. Earlier, in Kyoto, he helped his brother with paintings for Nijo Castle and the temple Chion-in.
credit_line: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III

meta: Sleep, a winged male nude by Jean Bernard Restout, shown first as Morpheus in 1783.
about: A nude man lies asleep with wings, poppies at his side. Jean Bernard Restout began with a studio study of the male body, a standard exercise for artists. By adding the wings and poppies he turned it into a more specific subject. He first showed it in a privately organized exhibition in 1783 under the title Morpheus, the god of sleep. The Cleveland Museum of Art says Ovid's Metamorphoses probably inspired him, since Ovid places the god of sleep in a cave with poppies at the entrance.

meta: Winter landscape: a ravine, an ink hanging scroll by Kano Hogai shown in Japan in 1884.
about: Snow lies in a ravine of jagged cliffs, with a rushing stream and windswept pines on rocky outcrops. The upper part of the scroll is left largely empty, like mist. The museum ties the evening landscape to Kano Hogai's study of earlier ink painters, among them Sesshu. It points to strong contrasts of ink tone and a reduction of detail that makes the image somewhat abstract. This landscape was exhibited in Japan in 1884, in the Second Competitive Show for the Promotion of National Painting sponsored by the Meiji government.

meta: Portrait of a Sculptor by Jean Baptiste Santerre, bequeathed to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1954.
about: A man in a gold turban-like headwrap and a loose grey robe over a white ruffled shirt turns toward the viewer with a faint smile. He holds a small tool near his lace cuff, which is why the sitter is called a sculptor. The painting was with the Vermeer Gallery in London by 1931. Max Epstein of Chicago bought it in 1935, and he bequeathed it to the Art Institute in 1954. Jean Baptiste Santerre painted it about 1705.

meta: Maria Gansevoort Melvill, painted about 1815 by Ezra Ames and given to the National Gallery of Art in 1947.
about: A seated woman in a black dress rests her cheek on one hand against a red drape. Lace trims her collar and her short sleeves, and she wears a gold jewelled hair ornament and earrings. The sitter lived from 1791 to 1872, and the portrait passed to her granddaughter Charlotte Elizabeth Hoadley in Chicago. The dealer C.W. Lyon sold it in 1917 to the collector Thomas B. Clarke. After his estate was sold, the A.W. Mellon Educational and Charitable Trust bought it in 1936 and gave it to the gallery.

meta: Charlotte Bonaparte's self-portrait of 1824, bought by the Princeton University Art Museum in 2023.
about: Charlotte Bonaparte shows herself seated in a green dress with puffed sleeves, a gold pen held over a drawing board with a pencil sketch of a building. A pearl and gold headband crosses her hair, and she looks straight at the viewer. She lived from 1802 to 1839. The picture passed by descent to her sister Zénaïde and to Charles Lucien Bonaparte, and stayed in the family until 2021. Two dealers handled it before Princeton bought it in 2023.

meta: A soldier and two hanged men, a book illustration drawn by Maynard Dixon in 1900.
about: A half-length soldier faces right with a rifle and fixed bayonet at his side. Behind him stand other figures in high silk hats. Silhouetted above rocks at the right background are two hanged men. Maynard Dixon drew it as a book illustration, in black ink with white highlights on tan paper, and dated it 1900.

meta: The New Song, a household scene by Jan Josef Horemans II with a woman playing a harpsichord.
about: A young woman at the left plays a song from a songbook on a harpsichord, while others sit at a table drinking tea. Two men smoke pipes. She has a foot warmer under her feet. In the background an old man is pawing a young woman. At the right a screen stands before the fireplace, with a coat and hat hanging from it, and a birdcage hangs from the ceiling. Jan Josef Horemans signed the painting at the lower left.

meta: The Sleeping Shepherd, a landscape of 1678 by Jan van der Meer II, signed on a pamphlet.
about: A shepherd boy in a red jacket sleeps on the ground beside a dog, with sheep resting and grazing near a large oak. His hat lies next to him, and so does an illustrated pamphlet. The painter signed and dated the work on that pamphlet, in the lower right corner, with the year 1678. A wooded hillside and a distant mountain fade into a warm, cloudy sky.

meta: Gilles Paul Cauvet's design for a bedroom in the Hotel de Mailly-Nesle in Paris, showing only the main wall.
about: Three steps lead up to an alcove with a bed at its centre, framed by a drapery that two female statues pull back. Unevenly spaced columns carry the entablature in front. Four candelabra stand between them, each made of a warrior and a girl holding trays with candlesticks. Reliefs ornament the wall behind. At the top, part of a curved ceiling shows two captives, trophies of weapons, putti and a segment of a painting. A scale at the bottom is marked 12 Pieds.

meta: Basket of Pears and Crabapples by John F. Francis, given to the National Gallery of Art in 2018 by the family of the scholar William H. Gerdts.
about: A woven basket lies tipped over on a white draped table and spills pears, crabapples and an apple. A red-striped cloth hangs against the dark background. The painting belonged to William H. Gerdts of New York by at least 1965. That year he lent it to an exhibition of the American Federation of Arts in New York. It came to the National Gallery of Art as a gift in 2018.
credit_line: Gift of William and Abigail Gerdts

meta: A two-fold gold screen of spring and autumn flowers attributed to Watanabe Shiko, with hollyhocks, poppies and morning glories.
about: Spring and autumn flowers share one gold ground on this two-fold paper screen. White wisteria and a wild chrysanthemum fill the upper right panel. Red and white poppies grow below them. In the left panel, lilies and white bush clover sit above morning glories. Miscanthus reeds tie the two panels together. Chinese bellflowers and a melon grow at the bottom. A signature and a square seal appear at the lower left. The museum says the bright colours and simple composition recall the Rimpa school.
